summary:
We developed the concept of a smart textile mesh that continuously monitors astronauts’ skin to give early warning of bacterial colonization and biofilm risk. The garment measures skin pH, impedance and temperature. It focuses on high-risk sentinel zones (armpits, groin, harness area, lower back and sacrum), and when one shows a sustained deviation, the alert extends to the surrounding zones. An accelerometer tells rest from exercise so that sweat doesn’t trigger false alarms. Alerts appear as a color change in the fabric and as a message to the spacecraft tablet.

The project addresses the closed-environment hazard and the host-microorganism interactions risk defined by NASA’s Human Research Program. On the ISS, skin rashes are the most frequently reported clinical event and are rarely confirmed in flight. Catching problems before symptoms appear lets the crew manage them with hygiene and monitoring, saves antibiotics and increases medical autonomy on missions to the Moon and Mars. The same technology could protect patients at risk of skin infection on Earth.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Starmesh is a smart textile mesh that continuously monitors astronauts’ skin to give early warning of bacterial colonization and biofilm risk. The garment measures three signals directly on the skin: pH, with polyaniline yarn; impedance, with silver textile electrodes; and temperature, with thermistors. It focuses on eight high-risk sentinel zones: armpits, groin, shoulders under the harness, lower back and sacrum. Each zone learns the astronaut’s personal baseline, and when one shows a sustained deviation, the alert extends to the neighboring zones. An accelerometer in the removable module distinguishes rest from exercise, so that sweat does not trigger false alarms. Alerts are delivered in two ways: a color change in the fabric itself, and a Bluetooth message to the spacecraft tablet showing the zone, alert level and trend.

Benefits
It catches the problem before symptoms appear, in the first hours of biofilm formation, when it can still be managed with hygiene and monitoring. This saves antibiotics from the spacecraft’s limited medical kit, avoids building up resistance in a closed environment, and gives the crew medical autonomy without depending on Earth.

Expected impact
On the ISS, skin rashes are the most frequently reported clinical event and are rarely confirmed in flight. Starmesh addresses the closed-environment hazard and the host-microorganism interactions risk defined by NASA’s Human Research Program. It is designed for missions to the Moon and Mars, and on Earth it could help bedridden patients, people at risk of skin infection and people in isolated environments.

Tools used
NASA resources (Human Research Program: hazards, risks and ongoing research) and CSA resources; scientific literature on biofilms and textile sensors; a previous textile pH sensor prototype using polyaniline (work done before the hackathon); an interactive simulation of the mesh’s 27 zones built with [tool or language]; figures and video made with [tools].

What makes it creative?
It combines three physical signals in a full-body garment for healthy skin, something that had only been tested separately in wound dressings or in the lab. It also adds sentinel zones that pass the alert to their neighbors, and a context filter that knows when the astronaut is exercising. As a future vision, we propose antibodies attached to latex particles to identify which bacterium is causing the alert.

Factors our team considered
Ergonomics and no manual procedures. Since clothes are not washed on the ISS, we designed a disposable garment with a reusable module. We also considered electrical safety, biocompatibility, flammability, particle shedding in the cabin and health data privacy. We are open about the limitations: Starmesh is a risk alert, not a diagnosis, and the project is at the concept stage (TRL 2), with a five-phase validation plan.
